3451.prule: initial: primary stress on the first syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive (word-initial stress; the word-initial syllable is the stressed one)
3451.srule: Stated (Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977: 124, sec. 5.2): 'In verbs of more than three syllables secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Tertiary stress falls on the peak syllable of each rhythm unit after the primary stressed syllable until the penultimate syllable.... In all non-verbs the secondary stress falls on the peak of every rhythm unit after the primary stress.' Rhythm units (sec. 5.1) are basically disyllabic; odd-numbered non-verbs end in a one-syllable unit and odd-numbered verbs have a three-syllable unit before the penult, so non-verbs carry a stress on every odd syllable (['ǽni"bǽni"báː] 'rainbow', ['ubu"dʒubu"dʒáː] 'sweet potato') while verbs of 5/7 syllables are stressed 1-4 / 1-3-6 (['bařpʰiːnán"tʰine] 'I just awoke', [tʰářpʰiː"'neřǽdʒi"maːgo] 'we awoke yesterday'); even lengths are 1-3(-5-7) in both classes.

3451.sec_rule: Rhythmic secondary stress by rhythm unit (Fleischmann & Turpeinen 1977, Kunini dialect): in non-verbs a secondary stress falls on the peak (first syllable) of every rhythm unit after the primary stress, rhythm units being two syllables with a one-syllable unit word-finally in odd-syllabled words (['dage"pʰledžʷa] 'bird sp.' 1010, ['æni"bæni"ba:] 'rainbow' 10101); in verbs of more than three syllables the secondary stress falls on the penultimate syllable and a tertiary stress on the peak of each rhythm unit between the primary and the penult, odd-syllabled verbs having a three-syllable unit immediately before the penult (['barpʰi:nan"tʰine] 'I just awoke' 10010, ['džemle:'''melæ"džiye] 'you (pl.) tied one thing' 101010). Words of up to three syllables are a single rhythm unit with the primary stress only; each stem of a compound carries its own initial primary stress.

3455.exq_: No stress rule, so no exceptions; for the tone system the source lists four processes (p. 91): 'We have observed four tonal processes: 1. LH is realized as L 2. Final L tones fall 3. L tone spread 4. Restriction on L + L'.
3455.tone: Morris 2016 argues for two level tones (H, L) and four melodies (H, HL, L, LH) in Bissa Barka, established by a two-week card-sorting session with Garango speakers (250 words) and by contexts that distinguish LH from L; she reviews the earlier disagreement (two tones: Hidden 1982 with downstep, Galbane 1985, Vanhoudt 1992; three tones: Prost 1950, Zouré 1975, Bambara 1980, Monet 1989) and explicitly rejects the WALS 13A 'No tones' coding as a misreading of Naden 1973's silence on tone. The one accentual proposal, Schreiber 2000: 60 (pitch-accent rather than tone), is reported second-hand and not adopted; no source opened gives a word-stress position. Family-level, the Jazyki Mira 2017 Mande overview (p. 34, held excerpt) says stress is absent in most Mande languages and singles out Bisa as reducible to a two-level tone system.

3459.heavy: Not applicable to the rule: the source states that all underlying syllables are light (no length contrast, no underlying diphthongs or codas) and that the language counts syllables (syllabic trochees, quantity-insensitive). Surface heavy syllables exist only as derived forms: a surface diphthong (from hiatus resolution) can form a foot on its own word-finally, which is how [da.ˈtau] keeps its stress; surface CVC from final-vowel deletion never attracts stress.
3459.prule: Main stress on the penultimate syllable of the underlying phonological word, quantity-insensitive (all underlying syllables are light; the language counts syllables): disyllabic left-headed feet (syllabic trochees) built right to left, End Rule Right picks the rightmost foot, an odd-syllabled word leaves its initial syllable unfooted. Surface final stress arises only when the stressed penult vowel fuses with a following vowel into a surface diphthong (/da.ˈta.u/ -> [da.ˈtau]); final-vowel deletion does not move stress.
3459.srule: Secondary stress on the head of every non-final foot: syllabic trochees built right to left from the main-stressed penult, each foot left-headed, so secondary stress falls on every second syllable leftward from the penult (four syllables ˌσσˈσσ: ma.za.ˈɣa.ni, fa.ka.ˈkra.ŋɔ, [`fa.ka=ˈniɣɔ]; five syllables σˌσσˈσσ: fu.fu.ɣɔ.ˈɡa.e); odd-syllabled words leave the initial syllable unfooted and unstressed.

3463.prule: Tone language (three tones in Burton-Page 1955; two in Joseph & Burling 2006, Samy 2011 and Das 2017); no phonological description since 1955 states a word-stress rule, and Burton-Page excludes stress from his analysis in principle. The fullest stress-placement statement is Endle 1884, written before tone was recognised (Skrefsrud 1889, Ch. I Section III 'Of accentuation', p. 5, adds for the Mech of Goalpara that in words of two syllables the penult and in words of three syllables the antepenult is 'generally' accented, 'adjectives commencing with g' and 'words ending with an abrupt semiconsonant' excepted, with 'also some other exceptions'): in words carrying no written accent 'the stress of the voice always rests on the first syllable of a word' (fai'dang, fai'dangman, mo'sá), explicitly independent of vowel quantity (quantity-insensitive); in words of more than two syllables the accent 'as a general rule' rests on the penultimate. Sub-rules and exceptions as Endle lists them: adjectives in ultra-short gă- accent the second syllable 'almost always' (găzá'); a declined noun 'sometimes' shifts the accent to its second syllable (Mo'sá > Mosá'ni); verbs 'for the most part retain their original accent (first syllable) throughout their conjugation' (khat'-bai 'ran'; cf. fai'dangman), but in compound verbs the second member 'usually' takes it; polysyllabic verb roots accent their second syllable 'almost always' (ga-glai'-nŭ, ge-le'-nŭ); the enclitics nŭ and sŭi draw the accent onto the syllable immediately preceding them (ga-glai'-nai ~ ga-glai-nai'-sŭi). Endle's rules do not reduce to a single penult rule for the inflected word.
3463.srule: Endle 1884 marks two degrees of accent in words of several syllables, a main accent (double mark) and a secondary accent (single acute); no rule for the position of the secondary accent is stated (it is marked word by word); the one worked example, Thang'-ni-au''-nŭ 'even while going', has the secondary accent on the first syllable and the main accent on the third, the syllable before the enclitic nŭ.

3463.tone: Burton-Page 1955 (Gauhati speaker), p. 341 §2.00-2.1: “Features considered as having no place are tone, intonation (pitch) and stress... Of the unplaced features, intonation and stress are more conveniently considered as abstractions from units longer than the syllable, and are thus excluded in principle from this paper, although the results of a study of these are implicit in the tonal categories which have been set up.” Three tones postulated (Tone 1 clear/tense/short, Tone 2, Tone 3); pp. 336-337 §§1.100, 1.130: “In unstressed syllables it has been necessary to recognize only one front vowel, written i in an initial syllable which bears no tone-mark... a voiceless tense front vowel of very short duration” (pi’sa ‘son’, si’kla ‘young girl’; likewise u in ku’ga ‘bird’s beak’). Samy 2011 LSI West Bengal p. 522 (§2.2): tone as suprasegmental phoneme, two-fold rising/falling; no stress. Das 2017 (abstract): two-tone language, lexical tones right-aligned within a minimal disyllabic prosodic word; Ch. 3 §3.2 'Stress in Boro', pp. 62-63: no consistent difference of duration or intensity between the two syllables of disyllabic words, 'stress is negligible in Boro'. 3465.tone: Four phonological level tones: ultra-high (double acute), high (acute), low (grave), ultra-low (double grave); minimal sets gba̋ 'leg' / gbá 'gift' / gbà 'door', pa̋ 'sting' / pá 'fill' / pȁ 'full'. Every vowel and the syllabic nasal /ŋ/ is a tone-bearer (p. 1053 n. 4). Tones combine within the word in practically any sequence (ba̋a̋, ba̋à, báá, báà, báȁ, bȁa̋, bȁá, bȁȁ). Contextual tone changes under close syntactic bond: ultra-high of a second element lowers to high when no ultra-high syllable is adjacent; ultra-high of the first element of an attributive NP lowers to low (kpɛ̋ 'house' -> kpɛ̀ bóóló 'round house'); an NP (even monosyllabic) cannot end in ultra-low. Grammatical tone: perfective by replacing the verb's lexical tone with ultra-low (bɔ́ 'go out' -> Bı̋ɔ́ bɔ̏ 'Bio went out'). Intonation limited: yes/no question = lengthened final vowel with ultra-low tone; clarifying question = tripled final vowel, last two vowels high or ultra-high. Nasalization is a syllable-level prosody. Sec. 1.4.0 table 1 gives the tone notations of Prost, Jones and this chapter. No stress or accent is mentioned anywhere except the explicit denial in 2.1.2.

3466.prule: Tone language, no stress rule. Every syllable of a word carries its own contrastive pitch; Table 1 of the 2017 paper (p. 169) uses only the three levels high, mid and low and their combinations (kayang HH 'small animal' / HL 'an idiot' / ML 'a mosquito'; dibe LH 'cola' / LM 'marriage' / LL 'shoe'; abe H 'cola-nuts' / L 'shoes' / M 'marriages'; be L 'come' / H 'marry' / M 'we'). A falling tone appears only in the companion book Bisong & Onucheyo 2020 (p. 10: 'Be (we) low tone, Be (marry) high tone, Be (come) falling tone'), which conflicts with the 2017 table on both 'come' (falling vs low) and 'we' (low vs mid). Tone distinguishes lexical items and, on verbs, TAM and negation. Stress is described only for English; the authors treat 'tone in Bokyi' as the functional counterpart of 'stress in English'. No position of word stress is given and no explicit denial of stress is made.

3466.tone: Source describes Bokyi as a tone language with per-syllable lexical tone at three levels, high, mid and low (Table 1, pp. 169-170: kayang HH 'small animal' / HL 'an idiot' / ML 'a mosquito'; dibe LH 'cola' / LM 'marriage' / LL 'shoe'; abe H/L/M; be L 'come' / H 'marry' / M 'we'; onang HH/LL/ML); no falling or contour tone is given for Bokyi (the paper's only 'falling' is the Mandarin ma example, p. 168). Verbs are 'basically tonal' (pp. 170-171): H on the final vowel = 3sg present, H on initial + L on final vowel = past perfective, L on final vowel = past imperfective, level tone / long initial vowel = negative; only the progressive takes a prefix (okuo-). The tone-language classification is attributed to Tawo 1977:126 via Oshita 2004:107. Stress not discussed in the source. 'stress' occurs only for English (p. 173). The companion book Bisong & Onucheyo 2020 (p. 10) gives be 'come' as falling and 'we' as low, conflicting with the 2017 table.

I am quite unable to deal, and at anyrate one which is outside the scope of this book... it is quite certain that tone cannot be learned from a book'). 3474.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Najamba is a tone language: every regular stem carries a lexical tone melody (/H/, /LH/, /HL/ or /LHL/, one or rarely two H elements, never all-L), which inflectional suffixes and syntactic constructions override with tone overlays.
3474.srule: Not mentioned in Heath 2017 (§2.1 Prosody p. 9; §3.1.2-3.1.3 p. 17; §3.6 Tones pp. 40-51; §3.7 Intonation p. 52): the grammar states no word stress at all, hence no secondary stress; its only metrical remark is that Najamba 'shows relatively little of the metrical patterning' of northern Dogon and that 'stem-final is not a metrically defined position in the usual sense'.
3474.quote: Najamba is a tonal language. H is high tone, L is low tone. Syllables may be H, L, falling <HL>, rising <LH>, or bell-shaped <LHL>. All regular stems (nouns, verbs, adjectives, numerals) have a lexical tone melody with one (rarely two) H-tone element(s). Some stems have /H/ lexical tone melody, others have /LH/, /HL/, or /LHL/ melody, spread out over the relevant number of syllables, but none is lexically all-L toned. These lexical melodies are modified or overridden by tone overlays imposed by inflectional suffixes (verbs) or by syntactic constructions (nouns, adjectives, numerals). [p. 9] .…

3474.tone: The grammar never states a word-stress or accent rule. 'stress' occurs once in the whole text, in an etymological aside ('the particle probably originated as an unstressed ‘there’ adverb', ch. 11); 'accent' only as a tone-mark term; 'pitch' only in intonation remarks (§3.7). §3.1.2 'Embryonic metrical structure' (p. 17) says Najamba shows little of the metrical (second-syllable vowel-reduction) patterning of northern Dogon and that 'stem-final is not a metrically defined position in the usual sense'; §3.1.3 (p. 17) says the light/heavy stem distinction 'is less important in Najamba than in some other Dogon languages... This is not a matter of weight per se.' Prosody is lexical tone melody plus grammatical tone overlays (tonosyntax).
